title: Hyrcanus and his brother Aristobulus
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: Hyman writes: The sons of King Yannai, whose mother was the great woman known as Queen Shelamzion, sister of Shimon ben Shetach, whose reign was the happiest period for Israel in all the days of the Second Temple. When she died, her two sons began to quarrel over the kingship, and they themselves handed the people of Israel over to the mighty Pompey, general of the Roman army, and brought destruction upon the people. This is mentioned in [Sotah 49b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sotah.49b.8-9): Our Rabbis taught: When the Hasmonean kings besieged one another, Hyrcanus was outside and Aristobulus inside. Each day they would lower denarii in a basket and haul up the daily offerings for them. There was an old man there who was versed in Greek wisdom. He said to them (the besiegers): As long as they carry out the Temple service, they will not be delivered into your hands. The next day — they hauled up a pig for them. When it reached halfway up the wall, it dug its claws into the wall and the Land of Israel shook four hundred parasangs. Hyman interprets this as meaning that then the entire Land of Israel was delivered into the hands of the swine. And [Rashi](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Song_of_Songs.6.12), in his holy language, says at the end of chapter 6 of Song of Songs, on the verse "I knew not my soul; it set me among the chariots of my princely people" ([Song of Songs 6:12](https://www.sefaria.org/Song_of_Songs.6.12)), that the dispute that grew strong among the Hasmonean kings Hyrcanus and Aristobulus was such that one of them brought Roman rule upon them and became its servant; Hyman adds that his end was that Herod killed him when he was an old man of more than eighty years.

notes.text: Hyman’s praise of the queen’s reign and his interpretation of the swine episode as Roman subjugation remain his prose. The referent of the final Herod/over-eighty pronoun remains unresolved; no modern historical harmonization is imposed.

The linked Sotah passage identifies Hyrcanus as the besieger and Aristobulus as the one inside the city. Hyman gives the political significance of the pig episode and his assessment of Queen Shelamzion’s reign.

The linked Rashi says that one of the brothers brought in Rome, took the kingship from it and became its servant. The three digital comments on this verse contain no statement about Herod killing either brother at over eighty. That final clause is Hyman’s report, with its referent left open.
